content: The Alere Determine™ TB LAM Ag test, commonly referred to as Alere LAM, is a commercially available point-of-care diagnostic tool designed to detect active tuberculosis (TB). This test is particularly useful in individuals living with HIV, especially those with advanced disease. The test operates as an immunocapture assay that identifies the lipoarabinomannan (LAM) antigen in urine. LAM is a lipopolysaccharide component of the mycobacterial cell wall, which is released from metabolically active or degenerating mycobacterial cells during TB infection. To perform the test, 60 µL of urine is manually applied to the test strip, specifically on the white pad marked with arrow symbols. The strip is then incubated at room temperature for 25 minutes. After incubation, the test strip is visually inspected for the presence of visible bands. The intensity of any visible band is graded by comparing it to a manufacturer-supplied reference scale card. This grading determines the positivity of the test result. The Alere LAM test is not intended to replace other diagnostic tests but is recommended for use in combination with existing diagnostic methods, particularly in the context of HIV-associated TB. The test is simple to use, requires minimal training, and is stable for up to 15 months at 30°C. It does not rely on sputum samples, which are often difficult to obtain in certain populations, but instead uses urine, a safer and more easily accessible specimen. The World Health Organization (WHO) has reviewed the diagnostic accuracy of Alere LAM for TB detection in people living with HIV (PLHIV). The test has shown varying sensitivity and specificity depending on the clinical setting and patient population. For HIV-positive adults presenting with TB symptoms, the sensitivity in inpatient settings is 52% (40–64%), with a specificity of 87% (78–93%). In outpatient settings, the sensitivity is lower at 29% (17–47%), but the specificity is higher at 96% (91–99%). Across all settings, the pooled sensitivity is 42% (31–55%), and the specificity is 91% (85–95%). For HIV-positive adults irrespective of TB symptoms, the sensitivity in inpatient settings is 62% (41–83%), with a specificity of 84% (48–96%). In outpatient settings, the sensitivity is 31% (18–47%), and the specificity is 95% (87–99%). Across all settings, the pooled sensitivity is 35% (22–50%), and the specificity is 95% (89–98%). In adults with advanced HIV disease (CD4 cell count ≤200), the sensitivity and specificity of Alere LAM vary by setting. In inpatient settings, the sensitivity is 64% (35–87%), and the specificity is 82% (67–93%). In outpatient settings, the sensitivity drops to 21% (8–48%), but the specificity remains high at 96% (89–99%). For those with CD4 counts ≤100, the sensitivity in inpatient settings is 57% (33–79%), with a specificity of 90% (69–97%). In outpatient settings, the sensitivity is 40% (20–64%), and the specificity is 87% (68–94%). For HIV-positive children, data on the diagnostic accuracy of Alere LAM is limited. Sensitivity and specificity vary across studies and settings. For example, in one outpatient study, the sensitivity was 42% (15–72%), and the specificity was 94% (73–100%). In an inpatient study, the sensitivity was 56% (21–86%), and the specificity was 95% (90–98%). The test has been shown to address a critical diagnostic need in populations where TB is challenging to diagnose. It is considered easy to use, rapid, and does not require sophisticated equipment or maintenance. However, challenges such as stock-outs, limited shelf life, and delays in initiating treatment after obtaining results have been reported. Despite these challenges, the benefits of the Alere LAM test, particularly in resource-limited settings and among vulnerable populations, outweigh its limitations. The test is also considered cost-effective, especially in hospitalized HIV-positive adults in high TB/HIV burden countries.
